system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2126-05-10 21:44:00 to 2126-05-20 17:52:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy, and functional quadriplegia was admitted with fever, tachycardia, and increased respiratory secretions. He was diagnosed with sepsis due to healthcare-associated pneumonia, likely from Klebsiella pneumoniae, and treated with IV cefepime and oral linezolid. His symptoms resolved, and labs improved. A concurrent Enterococcus faecium urinary finding was considered colonization but covered by linezolid. His home medications were continued, except citalopram, which was held due to interaction risk and scheduled for restart post-antibiotics. He was discharged to extended care with a plan to complete antibiotics and resume normal care.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

FINDINGS:

NECK, THORACIC INLET, AXILLAE, CHEST WALL: No suspicious thyroid lesions. 
Tracheostomy in situ.  Subcentimeter supraclavicular lymph nodes.  No axillary
adenopathy.  No gross breast lesions.  Right prepectoral Port-A-Cath in situ

UPPER ABDOMEN: This study was not tailored to evaluate the subdiaphragmatic
organs.  No adrenal lesions.  Possible small hiatal hernia.  Gastrostomy tube
in situ with its metallic tip seen in the proximal duodenum.  Multiple
subcentimeter calcified gallstones, no features of cholecystitis.

MEDIASTINUM: Subcentimeter mediastinal lymph nodes.

HILA: Mild hilar fullness (on this noncontrasted study) suggesting mild
adenopathy.

HEART and PERICARDIUM: Normal cardiac configuration.  No pericardial effusion.
No aortic valve or coronary artery calcifications.  No aneurysmal dilatation
of the ascending aorta.
PLEURA: Bilateral small nonhemorrhagic pleural effusions.
LUNG:

-PARENCHYMA:  Motion artifact degrades the evaluation of the pulmonary
parenchyma for small nodules and fine interstitial changes.  The most salient
change is the interval development of marked bronchial wall thickening without
overt bronchiectasis in both upper lobes (5, 72) and left lower lobe (5, 155).
Chronic, diffuse, coarse interstitial thickening with peripheral traction
bronchiectasis and architectural distortion shows mild interval progression
since ___.  Superimposed increased lung attenuation may represent
fibrosis under the resolution of CT, or pulmonary edema.  Multiple scattered
thin-walled cysts.  Mild apical paraseptal emphysema.

contain minimal secretions for example in the main bronchi bilateral (3, 25). 
Mild diffuse cylindrical bronchiectasis.  Diffuse subpleural bronchiolectasis.

pulmonary hypertension.

progression of the T11 insufficiency type fracture.  T7 insufficiency type
fracture is unchanged.  No lytic/destructive bony lesions.

thickening in the upper lobes and left lower lobe, probably inflammatory, due
to bronchial infection or perhaps aspiration.

Small bilateral pleural effusions are new.

fibrosis below the resolving capability of CT or normal in the setting of
small bilateral pleural effusions, interstitial pulmonary edema.   Viral
infection or PCP are not excluded.

Chronic fibrotic interstitial lung disease demonstrates mild interval
progression.


No focal airspace consolidation to suggest bacterial pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___ and I’ll be part of your care team. You’re here because of trouble breathing, fever, and high heart rate. We’re going to help you get through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not able to speak right now because of your trach, but we’ll work with your sister later if needed. For now, I’ll explain what’s going on and what we’re doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show a high white blood cell count, which means your body is fighting an infection. Your sodium is high, and your kidney function is a bit off. We think this is from dehydration and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Frown.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Don’t worry—we’re giving you fluids and antibiotics. You got meropenem and linezolid tonight to cover possible pneumonia and a resistant infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray shows long-standing lung changes, but no new pneumonia yet. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a central line in your neck yesterday to give antibiotics safely. That will help us treat you better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Raise eyebrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s in your right internal jugular vein and goes into your heart. It’s secure and working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a bronchoscopy yesterday to get samples from your lungs. It was safe, and we sent the fluid for testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The results came back. You have Klebsiella and two types of Pseudomonas in your lungs. One Pseudomonas is resistant to some antibiotics, but we’re using meropenem and will switch to cefepime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Frown.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on top of it. Cefepime works well against this bug. You’ll get it through your IV for 7 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also found Enterococcus faecium in your urine. It’s resistant to vancomycin, but linezolid covers it. You’re finishing that course now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan shows thickened airway walls, likely from infection or aspiration. No focal pneumonia, so we’re on the right track with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw small pleural effusions—fluid around the lungs. They’re not large, so we’re not draining them. They may be from infection or heart strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Raise eyebrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch them. Your heart looks okay, but your lung disease makes it harder to tell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Your fever is gone, and your breathing is easier. Your blood pressure is still on the lower side, but that’s your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smile slightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on cefepime. It’s important to finish the full course to fully treat the Pseudomonas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started a scopolamine patch to help reduce your lung secretions. It’s changed every 3 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—great sign the antibiotics are working. Your kidney function is also improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still giving your home meds—Keppra for seizures, your HIV meds, and vancomycin for C. diff prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your citalopram while on linezolid because they can interact. We’ll restart it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line in your left arm yesterday for long-term antibiotics. The X-ray confirms it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning for discharge in a few days once antibiotics are complete.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on day 5 of cefepime. Two more doses to go. Your breathing is stable, and you’re off pressors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We added a lidocaine patch for your right thigh pain. How’s that helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thumbs up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We did a swallow study today. No aspiration seen—good news. You may be able to eat by mouth again at your facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smile widely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue tube feeds for now, but this is a positive step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost done. One more dose of cefepime tomorrow. Your labs are nearly normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your citalopram tomorrow. And keep taking oral vancomycin for two more weeks after antibiotics end.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today to your extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the cefepime today. Keep the scopolamine patch and lidocaine patch as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Restart citalopram today. Continue oral vancomycin until two weeks after cefepime ends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with pulmonology for your lung condition. Your sister has all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. We’re proud of your progress. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nod, then weak thumbs up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy, and functional quadriplegia was admitted with septic shock and respiratory distress. He was found to have ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa, treated with a 7-day course of meropenem followed by cefepime. A vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium urinary infection was covered by linezolid. His sepsis resolved, and he improved clinically with stable vitals and reduced secretions. He was discharged to extended care with plans to complete cefepime, continue oral vancomycin for C. diff prophylaxis, restart citalopram, and follow up with pulmonology.
